A motor dealer selling its own vehicles and introducing buyers to third-party finance may qualify for limited-permission secondary credit broking. That is a starting point, not a rule for every dealer. The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) route depends on stock ownership, agreement types, sourcing, part-exchanges and other regulated activities—not simply the size of the business.

The FCA sets separate conditions for finance introductions connected to a vehicle-sourcing service. These include whether the introduction would happen without that service and whether most revenue comes from sourcing rather than the credit introductions. Settlement of existing vehicle finance also affects the permissions to consider.

A motor-dealer FCA application needs information about the firm, its ownership, proposed regulated activities and how it will operate. The FCA’s motor-dealer guidance specifically describes what it expects in a regulatory business plan. The complete document and form requirements depend on the permissions, legal structure and people involved.
Explain the business, customer journey, partners, risks and controls. Use the motor-dealer requirements below.

CCR009 is a regulatory return: information a firm submits to the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), not a licence or a tax return. Its formal name is the Relevant Ancillary Credit Firm return. It covers specified consumer-credit permissions, including credit broking, and asks about the firm’s activities and business. The questions shown depend on the firm’s answers.
Start with the current form and completion notes. Use the FCA’s data-flow diagrams to understand the route through the questions that applies to your business.

CCR009 and CCR007 are different FCA returns. CCR009 covers relevant ancillary credit firms; CCR007 is Key Data for Credit Firms with Limited Permissions. CCR009 replaces some CCR007 information, but relevant limited-permission firms can still need to submit both. Follow each return’s current instructions and schedule.

The FCA permits firms submitting CCR009 to report zero in CCR007 fields 1A and 3A where those fields relate only to credit broking or not-for-profit debt management. Where other limited-permission activities are carried on, accurate information for those activities is still needed. The remaining fields still require accurate information.

CCR007 is a key-data return and can include complaints information for limited-permission firms. It should not simply be renamed “the complaints return”. Other complaints-reporting requirements depend on the firm’s scope.

Prepare for CCR009 by confirming the reporting scope and deadline, arranging access, gathering evidence for the applicable questions and assigning responsibility for review and submission. A clear preparation process can reduce last-minute work without changing the firm’s FCA obligations.
The timetable below is a suggested internal workflow, not an FCA-prescribed preparation schedule. Set dates that leave room to resolve questions before your actual deadline.

The FCA says the firm’s Principal User has access to CCR009 and can grant other users the permissions needed to view, edit or submit it. Confirm the access each person actually needs. “Principal User” here is a RegData access role; it does not mean the firm is an appointed-representative principal.

CCR009 uses calendar-based reporting periods, with a 40-business-day submission window. Most firms report annually; some report twice a year. Check the exact period and due date on your firm’s My FCA schedule. The £5 million boundary and first reporting period need care because the FCA’s overview and Handbook wording are not fully aligned.
Annual credit-related regulated activity revenue of £5 million or less: 1 January–31 December.
